old: Choose first by cane type, then by hardiness and season. Summer-bearing (floricane) reds give one big early-summer crop on second-year canes and include the hardiest varieties for cold regions; everbearing (primocane) types fruit on first-year canes in late summer or fall and can be mowed to the ground each winter for the simplest pruning and a clean, single fall crop. Black and purple raspberries are summer-bearing, do not sucker, and are less hardy and more disease-prone than reds. In the hot, humid South, standard raspberries fail, and only heat-tolerant low-chill types such as Dorman Red are worth trying. Always start with certified virus-free stock.

old: Most raspberries need a stretch of winter chill (hours below about 45°F) to break dormancy and fruit normally. Standard red raspberries are high-chill, often needing 800 or more hours, which is why they fail in mild-winter regions; medium-chill types want 400 to 600, and a few heat-bred types such as Dorman Red need only about 300. Too little chill for the type gives weak, erratic budbreak and little fruit, so chill, alongside summer heat tolerance, is the main thing that limits where raspberries grow.

old: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie: the hot, low, alkaline core is the ground Utah State University Extension flags as difficult, and the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns instead. The best bet here is a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) type, because its fall crop ripens after the peak summer heat and avoids fruit sunburn (USU Extension); good choices are Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dorman Red. Give it afternoon shade, mulch heavily, correct the alkaline-soil iron chlorosis with a chelated iron, and water steadily.

old: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie core: this is a hot, low, alkaline-soil site, the kind Utah State University Extension flags as difficult for the crop, while the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns above the valley. The steer here is toward heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) types, and USU Extension's reasoning is a timing one: a primocane crop comes in on the far side of the summer peak, late enough that the fruit is not sitting through the worst of the desert sun, which is what scorches a summer-bearing crop. Look to the fall-bearing varieties Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dorman Red. Plant dormant canes in late winter, and expect the alkaline soil to drive iron chlorosis, so treat yellowing leaves with a chelated iron. Give the planting afternoon shade to cut sunburn, mulch the shallow roots, use raised beds in heavy soil, and water steadily through the dry heat. Even managed well, treat this as a hard-won, shorter-lived planting than a cooler climate would give.
